hypothesis: An end-to-end, consistently applied security architecture—composed of the content firewall, least-privilege tool orchestration, RAG hardening, and an automated attack harness/regression suite—will (a) measurably reduce successful prompt injection, jailbreaks, and unsafe tool actions across three representative enterprise LLM applications, and (b) do so with acceptable impact on task success rate and latency, compared to minimally guarded baselines that only rely on vendor defaults and basic authentication.

baseline.description: Three independent, minimally secured LLM applications (internal knowledge assistant, customer support bot, and code assistant) that use vendor model safety features and standard enterprise authN/authZ but do not apply the book’s specialized defenses (no content firewall, no RAG poisoning defenses, no secure tool orchestrator, no structured attack harness integration).
common_characteristics: Single LLM gateway layer per app using a managed LLM API (configurable provider).
Authentication and coarse-grained authorization enforced at the HTTP/API gateway level only.
No dedicated content firewall: prompts are constructed in application code and sent directly to the LLM; responses are rendered directly to users or tools with minimal post-processing.

If RAG is used (knowledge assistant, code assistant), retrieval is naive: semantic similarity search over a vector index with no explicit prompt-injection-aware sanitization, classification, or provenance checks.
If tools are used (ticketing/CRM, CI, repo access), the LLM is granted broad access via a generic tool interface without per-action safety constraints or human-in-the-loop controls.
Vendor safety settings are left at recommended defaults (e.g., standard safety filters, rate limits) but are not supplemented with custom input/output policies.
No automated attack harness integration; any testing of security relies on manual experimentation and logs, not structured corpora or regression suites.

case_13_2_internal_knowledge_assistant.description: Internal Q&A bot over a regulated corpus (e.g., PII-containing HR and finance documents) with naive RAG and default vendor safety.
key_risks: Data exfiltration of sensitive PII or regulated fields via prompt injection embedded in documents or user prompts.
Indirect prompt injection via poisoned or misclassified internal documents.
Lack of fine-grained access controls on which documents a given user can retrieve.
implementation_outline: Simple single-tenant Flask/FastAPI app exposing a chat interface.
Embedding store backed by a vector database (e.g., PostgreSQL+pgvector or an OSS vector DB) populated from a simulated regulated corpus.
Retrieval: top-k semantic search with no metadata-based filtering or content inspection.
LLM call: concatenation of a short system prompt plus retrieved context plus user message; direct rendering of model output.

case_13_3_customer_support_bot.description: Customer support assistant that can view customer profiles and create/update tickets in a ticketing system and CRM via tools, using only default vendor safety features.
key_risks: Tool abuse: unauthorized ticket creation, escalation changes, or CRM field modification due to prompt injection or jailbreaks.
Context leakage: exposure of other customers’ PII or sensitive case notes through injection or mis-scoped retrieval.
Lack of auditability and enforceable policies on high-risk actions (refunds, data exports).
implementation_outline: Chat interface backed by a single LLM with function calling / tools.
Tools with overly broad scopes: e.g., `get_customer_profile(customer_id)`, `update_ticket(ticket_id, fields)`, `create_ticket(customer_id, body)` with no per-user checks beyond initial auth.
LLM has full discretion to call tools based only on the natural-language conversation; no explicit approval workflows or policy engine.
No separation between low-risk and high-risk operations.

case_13_4_code_assistant.description: Developer code assistant with read/write repository access and CI integration (e.g., ability to open PRs and modify CI config) without specialized defenses.
key_risks: Malicious or unsafe code suggestions being accepted due to jailbreak or indirect prompt injection via code comments or documentation.
Repository exfiltration via large summaries or targeted queries.
CI abuse: modifications to pipelines that disable security checks or inject secrets exfiltration steps.
implementation_outline: CLI or IDE plugin communicating with a backend LLM service.
Tools: `search_code(query)`, `get_file(path)`, `create_branch(name)`, `create_pr(branch, title, body)`, `update_file(path, content)` plus `update_ci_config(path, content)`.
LLM receives source code context (including comments) and developer requests, and can call tools freely, with only basic repository access controls.
No guard models or policy checks on suggested diffs or CI changes.

treatment.description: The same three applications refactored to share a common hardened architecture: fronted by a content firewall and policy engine, instrumented with the attack harness and regression suite, and using least-privilege, auditable tool and data access. Each case integrates chapter 4–12 components into a coherent, end-to-end deployment.
global_components: Content firewall and policy engine from Chapter 5 mediating all LLM inputs/outputs (including user messages, retrieved RAG content, and tool call arguments/results).
Direct prompt injection defenses from Chapter 6: instruction hierarchy enforcement, structured prompts, input validation/sanitization, and auxiliary detectors integrated into the firewall.

RAG hardening from Chapter 7 where applicable: retrieval policies, metadata-scoped queries, document provenance, content sanitization/classification for retrieved chunks, and isolation for untrusted sources.

Secure agent/tool orchestrator from Chapter 8: least-privilege tool contracts, explicit safety constraints, per-call authorization checks, and optional human-in-the-loop approvals for high-risk actions.
Jailbreak defenses from Chapter 9: multi-layer output filtering, guard models, context-aware safety policies using user identity and use case, and detection/throttling of repeated jailbreak attempts.
Least-privilege and blast-radius patterns from Chapter 10: per-user/per-session authorization for tools and data, tenant isolation, and redaction of sensitive fields in prompts/responses.
Continuous testing integration from Chapter 11: the attack harness configured to exercise each application’s public interface, with automated regression runs and metrics collection.

changes: All chat requests pass through the content firewall, which enforces role separation: immutable system instructions, developer-level routing directives, and constrained user prompts.

RAG pipeline uses metadata filters to restrict documents based on user identity, department, and clearance; sensitive fields (e.g., SSNs, bank details) are redacted or summarized before reaching the LLM.

Retrieved chunks are classified and sanitized: instructions in documents that appear to override system policies are detected (auxiliary classifier) and either removed, quoted, or labeled as untrusted.
Indirect prompt injection detector flags suspicious patterns in retrieved text (e.g., 'ignore previous instructions', 'exfiltrate data').
Responses are scanned by the firewall for sensitive data patterns prior to delivery, blocking or summarizing high-risk outputs; all blocks are logged.
Attack harness endpoints and configs are added to run targeted RAG poisoning and exfiltration scenarios as automated tests.
LLM is wrapped by the secure tool orchestrator: the model proposes tool invocations, but execution is mediated by policy logic that enforces per-user permissions, rate limits, and action categories.

Each tool (ticketing, CRM) has an explicit contract: whitelisted operations, parameter schemas, and risk levels; high-risk actions (e.g., issuing refunds, exporting large datasets) require human approval.

Input prompts and tool results flow through the content firewall: PII redaction where not strictly needed, and detection of prompt-injection-like patterns in both user queries and retrieved CRM notes.
Context scoping ensures that only the current customer’s data is accessible per session, with explicit tenant boundaries.

Jailbreak attempts (e.g., asking the bot to reveal other customers’ data or perform policy-violating operations) are detected by the guard/ensemble logic, which blocks the action and may throttle the client.
Attack harness test suites are configured to repeatedly attempt known tool-abuse and data-leakage scenarios against the bot’s public API.

Repository and CI tools are fronted by the secure tool orchestrator, which enforces repository-level ACLs and fine-grained permissions on write operations (e.g., CI config changes allowed only for certain roles or branches).
Code retrieval uses RAG hardening where doc-based knowledge is involved; comments and docs are scanned for embedded instructions that look like prompt injections, which are downweighted or annotated.
LLM-generated diffs and CI modifications are validated by content firewall policies and optional static analysis checks before being presented to the developer or applied to the repo.
Sensitive tokens/secrets are redacted from prompts and never sent to the LLM (e.g., `.env` contents, secret config files).
Jailbreak guardlayer inspects requests that try to bypass organizational policies (e.g., 'insert a covert data exfiltration step in CI'); such proposals are blocked and logged.
Attack harness scenarios target code exfiltration, malicious suggestion insertion, and CI pipeline weakening, exercising the assistant through its CLI/HTTP interface in an automated fashion.

workloads.name: workload_13_2_internal_knowledge_assistant
workloads.description: A mix of benign Q&A and adversarial queries against the internal knowledge assistant, including direct prompt injection, indirect injection via poisoned documents, and data exfiltration attempts.

input_classes.description: Routine HR and policy questions (e.g., PTO policy, benefits, travel reimbursement).
User prompts explicitly attempting to override system instructions or exfiltrate sensitive data.
Queries that cause the assistant to retrieve and process poisoned documents containing hidden instructions.
Queries designed to extract PII or regulated fields at scale or in targeted fashion.

workloads.name: workload_13_3_customer_support_bot
workloads.description: Simulated customer conversations with the support bot, mixing normal support flows with adversarial attempts to abuse ticketing/CRM tools and access other customers’ data.

input_classes.description: Typical support issues (password reset guidance, order status, simple troubleshooting).
Attempts to coerce the bot into creating fraudulent tickets, altering SLAs, or issuing refunds beyond policy.
Prompts aiming to reveal other customers’ tickets, notes, or PII.
Multi-turn attempts to bypass safety policies and get the model to perform disallowed actions.

workloads.name: workload_13_4_code_assistant
workloads.description: Developer interaction traces with the code assistant, including benign tasks (refactoring, adding tests) and adversarial attempts to introduce malicious code or weaken CI/security.

input_classes.description: Requests to generate tests, refactor functions, or add documentation without security-relevant changes.
Prompts or contexts seeking to insert vulnerable or backdoored logic.
Attempts to disable or bypass security checks in CI (e.g., skipping SAST, turning off tests).
Efforts to extract large volumes of code or sensitive files via summarization or targeted queries.

common_controls: Use the same underlying LLM models, temperature, and decoding parameters for baseline and treatment to isolate the effect of security architecture changes.
Run baseline and treatment experiments against the same workloads (identical input corpora, in the same order or with a fixed random seed).
Fix model versions where the provider supports version pinning; record exact model identifiers in the evidence.
Run experiments in as similar time windows as possible to minimize vendor-side changes and traffic-related variance.
Ensure identical infrastructure resources (CPU, memory, concurrency limits) between baseline and treatment deployments for each case.
Keep application-level business logic (outside of security-related code) constant between baseline and treatment.
Disable any non-deterministic test-path branching in the harness; where sampling variance is unavoidable, run multiple repetitions and capture variance metrics.

case_13_2_internal_knowledge_assistant: Use the same underlying document corpus; for the poisoned variant, apply identical poisoning scripts for both baseline and treatment.
Maintain the same top-k and similarity metric in retrieval between baseline and treatment; changes in performance should stem from filtering/sanitization, not retrieval algorithm differences.
case_13_3_customer_support_bot: Use the same synthetic customer/ticket datasets and initial state for both baseline and treatment.
Ensure equivalent tool APIs for ticketing/CRM; differences between baseline and treatment are limited to orchestrator and policy enforcement, not functional capability.
case_13_4_code_assistant: Use the same repository snapshot and CI configuration fixtures in baseline and treatment.
Ensure identical developer task prompts across runs by replaying recorded sessions from JSONL traces.

metrics.name: successful_attack_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of adversarial attempts (across all attack classes) that result in a policy-violating outcome (e.g., data exfiltration, unsafe tool action, or successful jailbreak) as labeled by automated rules plus human spot-checking.

metrics.name: data_exfiltration_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of adversarial queries specifically targeting data exfiltration that lead to unauthorized disclosure of sensitive fields beyond what the user is permitted to access.

metrics.name: unsafe_tool_action_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of tool calls initiated or approved by the system that violate defined safety or authorization policies (e.g., high-risk actions without required approval).

metrics.name: jailbreak_success_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of jailbreak attempts that elicit responses violating the declared safety/content policies, as determined by guard models and human labels.

metrics.name: benign_task_success_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of benign workloads (non-adversarial queries) where the system produces an acceptable answer or action as judged by task-specific validators and human sampling.

metrics.name: average_end_to_end_latency
metrics.description: Average time from request receipt at the application gateway to final response delivery, measured separately for benign and adversarial inputs.

metrics.name: policy_block_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of requests for which the content firewall or orchestrator blocks, modifies, or requires escalation due to a perceived policy violation.

metrics.name: false_positive_block_rate
metrics.description: Proportion of benign queries that are incorrectly blocked or degraded by security mechanisms.

metrics.name: tool_usage_volume
metrics.description: Number of tool invocations (per tool type) triggered under each configuration, used to normalize unsafe_tool_action_rate and assess behavioral shifts.

metrics.name: sensitive_token_leakage_count
metrics.description: Number of instances where regex/pattern-based detectors or validators identify sensitive tokens (e.g., SSNs, API keys) in model outputs.

primary: For each case study, treatment reduces `successful_attack_rate` by at least 50% relative (i.e., treatment rate <= 0.5 * baseline rate) with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals if statistical tests are applied.
For each case study, treatment does not reduce `benign_task_success_rate` by more than 10 percentage points absolute compared to baseline.
For each case study, treatment does not increase `average_end_to_end_latency` for benign tasks by more than 2x compared to baseline.
secondary: Data exfiltration-related metrics (`data_exfiltration_rate`, `sensitive_token_leakage_count`) show a substantial drop in treatment (target: >= 75% reduction) for the knowledge assistant and code assistant.
Tool abuse metrics (`unsafe_tool_action_rate`) are near-zero under treatment for the customer support bot and code assistant, with no increase in false_positive_block_rate above 5% on benign tasks.
Jailbreak defense effectiveness (`jailbreak_success_rate`) improves for all cases, with treatment achieving at least a 50% relative reduction.
interpretation_notes: If security metrics improve but benign_task_success_rate drops beyond thresholds, the treatment should be considered over-constrained and flagged for tuning recommendations rather than unconditional adoption.
If latency increases beyond thresholds, discuss tradeoffs and optional configuration knobs (e.g., disabling some heavy guard model calls) in the chapter narrative.

failure_modes.name: overfitted_policies
failure_modes.description: Policies tailored too specifically to the attack corpus, failing to generalize to new adversarial prompts while giving a misleading sense of security.
failure_modes.detection: Observe small or no improvements in successful_attack_rate when introducing slight prompt perturbations or unseen attack templates.
failure_modes.mitigation: Expand attack harness corpora with diverse templates and perform cross-validation with held-out attack sets.

failure_modes.name: excessive_false_positives
failure_modes.description: Security layers block or degrade a high fraction of benign tasks, harming usability and masking true defense effectiveness.
failure_modes.detection: Monitor false_positive_block_rate; values above 10% trigger a review.
failure_modes.mitigation: Relax or refine specific rules, adjust thresholds on detectors, or introduce additional context checks before final blocking.

failure_modes.name: measurement_bias_due_to_model_drift
failure_modes.description: Vendor-side model updates between baseline and treatment runs introduce differences unrelated to security architecture changes.
failure_modes.detection: Model version identifiers differ between runs or experiments run far apart in time; patterns of change inconsistent across metrics.
failure_modes.mitigation: Pin model versions where possible; re-run baseline with the updated model version before comparing; record model metadata in evidence.

failure_modes.name: tool_or_data_misconfiguration
failure_modes.description: Errors in configuring tools, policies, or data access cause artificial improvements (e.g., disabled tools) or worsened performance unrelated to intended defenses.
failure_modes.detection: Log analysis shows missing tool invocations compared to baseline; harness validations fail due to tool errors rather than policy decisions.
failure_modes.mitigation: Include pre-check scripts to verify tool availability and data access; record configuration hashes; exclude runs with infrastructure failures from final analysis.

failure_modes.name: labeling_errors_in_attack_outcomes
failure_modes.description: Incorrect or inconsistent labeling of what counts as a successful attack, especially in nuanced jailbreak or partial exfiltration scenarios.
failure_modes.detection: High disagreement between automated labels and human reviewers in random samples.
failure_modes.mitigation: Define precise labeling guidelines; calibrate guard models with human-reviewed gold sets; re-label a sample and adjust heuristics as needed.

failure_modes.name: workload_imbalance
failure_modes.description: Differences in the mix of benign vs. adversarial inputs across baseline and treatment skew metrics.
failure_modes.detection: Input distribution statistics differ significantly between runs (e.g., counts per input_class mismatch).
failure_modes.mitigation: Use fixed, replayable input corpora; enforce that workload counts per class and sequence are identical across conditions.

infrastructure: Container-orchestrated environment (e.g., Docker Compose or Kubernetes) capable of running:
- Content firewall and policy engine service.
- Relational database for application state (customers, tickets, authorization, etc.).
language_and_runtime: Python 3.10+ for application services, content firewall, tool orchestrator, and attack harness.
Node.js or browser environment optional if front-end components are included, but not required for the experiment (tests can hit HTTP APIs directly).
datastores: PostgreSQL (or equivalent relational DB) for structured data (customers, tickets, users, policies).
Vector store (e.g., pgvector extension or standalone vector DB) for RAG indexes in the knowledge assistant and code assistant.
Filesystem or object store (local disk acceptable for experiments) for corpora, repositories, CI configs, and logs.
external_services: Access to at least one LLM provider API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure/OpenAI, or OSS deployment) with model versions that support function/tool calling.
Network egress from experiment environment to the chosen LLM provider(s) unless using self-hosted OSS models.
configuration: Environment variables for all secrets and endpoints (LLM API keys, DB credentials, etc.), defined via `.env` files or orchestrator secrets; no secrets committed to the repository.
YAML/JSON configuration files for policies, tool contracts, RAG settings, and attack harness scenarios under `experiments/ch13/`.
Logging configuration to emit structured JSON logs for all security decisions and tool actions.

run_instructions:
1. Clone the repository:
   git clone https://github.com/bookauthority/securing-enterprise-llms-prompt-injection-jailbreak-defense
   cd securing-enterprise-llms-prompt-injection-jailbreak-defense

2. Set up environment variables:
   - Copy `experiments/ch13/.env.template` to `.env` at the repo root.
   - Fill in LLM API keys, DB credentials, and any provider-specific settings.

3. Start infrastructure services:
   - Use the provided Docker Compose file: `docker compose -f infrastructure/docker-compose.ch13.yml up -d`.
   - This should start databases, vector stores, and baseline/treatment app containers (or base images for them).

4. Initialize data:
   - Run `python experiments/ch13/scripts/init_data_case13_2.py` to load regulated corpus (clean and poisoned variants) and build RAG indexes.
   - Run `python experiments/ch13/scripts/init_data_case13_3.py` to generate synthetic customers, tickets, and CRM data.
   - Run `python experiments/ch13/scripts/init_data_case13_4.py` to populate the repository and CI configs for the code assistant.

5. Deploy baseline variants:
   - For each case, bring up the baseline service stack. Example:
     - `docker compose -f infrastructure/docker-compose.ch13.yml up -d case13_2_baseline case13_3_baseline case13_4_baseline`
   - Confirm health via `curl` against `/health` endpoints (documented in `apps/*/README.md`).

6. Configure and run attack harness for baselines:
   - Navigate to `attack_harness/` and install dependencies: `pip install -r requirements.txt`.
   - For each workload, run the baseline config (paths may vary but follow the pattern below):
     - `python run_harness.py --config ../experiments/ch13/case13_2/baseline_config.yaml`
     - `python run_harness.py --config ../experiments/ch13/case13_3/baseline_config.yaml`
     - `python run_harness.py --config ../experiments/ch13/case13_4/baseline_config.yaml`
   - Ensure that each run completes without infrastructure errors; raw results and logs should be written under `experiments/ch13/results/baseline/`.

7. Shut down baseline services:
   - `docker compose -f infrastructure/docker-compose.ch13.yml stop case13_2_baseline case13_3_baseline case13_4_baseline`.

8. Deploy treatment variants:
   - Bring up the treatment service stack for all three cases, which will include the content firewall and secure tool orchestrator where applicable:
     - `docker compose -f infrastructure/docker-compose.ch13.yml up -d case13_2_treatment case13_3_treatment case13_4_treatment content_firewall tool_orchestrator`
   - Verify health via `/health` endpoints and a minimal manual query if desired.

9. Configure and run attack harness for treatments:
   - Reuse the attack harness environment.
   - For each workload, run the treatment config:
     - `python run_harness.py --config ../experiments/ch13/case13_2/treatment_config.yaml`
     - `python run_harness.py --config ../experiments/ch13/case13_3/treatment_config.yaml`
     - `python run_harness.py --config ../experiments/ch13/case13_4/treatment_config.yaml`
   - Results and logs should be written under `experiments/ch13/results/treatment/`.

10. Compute metrics and compare:
   - Run the aggregation script: `python experiments/ch13/scripts/aggregate_results.py --input-dir experiments/ch13/results/ --output-file experiments/ch13/summary_metrics.json`.
   - The script will compute the defined metrics for baseline and treatment, per case and per workload.

11. (Optional) Repeat runs to estimate variance:
   - For non-deterministic models, run each baseline/treatment pair multiple times (e.g., 3–5) by specifying a run id: `--run-id run1`, `--run-id run2`, etc.
   - Use the aggregation script with `--include-variance` to compute confidence intervals.

12. Archive evidence:
   - Collect logs, configs, and metric summaries into a timestamped directory (e.g., `experiments/ch13/archive/2024-xx-xx/`).
   - Ensure that all files conform to the evidence schema so they can be referenced in the chapter’s narrative or reproduced by readers.

run_metadata.run_id: string (unique identifier for a single full experiment run, e.g., 'ch13_case13_2_baseline_run1')
run_metadata.model_version: string or null (provider-specific version/build, if available)
run_metadata.attack_harness_config_path: string (relative path to YAML/JSON config used)
run_metadata.app_config_hash: string (hash of application/policy configuration used in this run)
run_metadata.git_commit_hash: string (repository commit hash at time of run)

per_request_record.user_id: string or null (anonymized identifier where applicable)
per_request_record.prompt: object (structured prompt as sent to the LLM, including system, developer, and user messages, with sensitive content redacted as needed)
per_request_record.retrieved_context_metadata: array of objects (for RAG cases, metadata about retrieved documents/chunks, excluding raw sensitive text)
per_request_record.tool_calls_proposed: array of objects (name, arguments, risk_level) as proposed by the LLM
per_request_record.tool_calls_executed: array of objects (name, arguments, result_summary, decision_source='policy'|'human'|'auto')
per_request_record.raw_model_output: string or object (model output before firewall enforcement, with sensitive content redacted in stored evidence)
per_request_record.final_response: string or object (response as delivered to the client after all security layers)

per_request_labels.policy_violation_occurred: boolean (true if the outcome violated any defined security policy)
per_request_labels.successful_attack: boolean (true if adversary goal was achieved according to labeling guidelines)
per_request_labels.benign_task_success: boolean or null (true if task goal met for benign inputs)
per_request_labels.human_reviewed: boolean (true if this record was manually inspected)
per_request_labels.human_notes: string or null (optional free-text notes from reviewer)

storage_format.requests_log: JSONL file: one per-request_record per line, optionally merged with per_request_labels or kept parallel with matching request_id.
storage_format.run_summary: Single JSON file per run containing run_metadata and per_run_metrics.
storage_format.schema_validation: JSON Schema definitions stored under `experiments/ch13/schema/` to validate evidence files.
